Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette:
Maya was twenty-six when it began, a second-grade teacher in a quiet suburban school. The man lived in the apartment next door. At first, it was just small things-notes left under her windshield wiper, a single red rose on her doormat. She told herself it was sweet, maybe a shy admirer. But then he started watching. She would see him standing at his window as she came home, his face half-lit in the dark. The notes became longer, more intimate, referencing things she had only said on the phone. The police were called three times. Twice they told her there wasn't enough to press charges. The third time, they found him in the basement stairwell, breathing heavily into the dark. That sound-that wet, deliberate breath-was the last thing she heard before she ran. She never saw his face clearly, but she could not stop hearing him.

Now, two years later, Maya lives in a new apartment across town, but the world has not become safe. The heavy breathing sounds still arrive without warning-a man jogging past her on the sidewalk, a student's father leaning in to whisper a thank-you after parent-teacher night. The moment she hears it, her chest locks, and she is back in that stairwell. The memory is not a story she can tell; it arrives in jagged pieces-the smell of damp concrete, the cold metal of the railing, the sound of his breath-and then it vanishes, leaving her disoriented and unable to explain to anyone why she has gone pale. She has tried to describe it to her boyfriend, but the words will not come. She knows what happened, but the shape of it dissolves the moment she tries to speak.

What frightens Maya most is not the memory itself but what it means. She has come to believe that people cannot be trusted-that anyone might be hiding something, that a stranger approaching her in the grocery store might be the beginning of something terrible. She scans every face, every pair of eyes that lingers too long. The silence in her classroom during a spelling test now feels ominous; she finds herself listening for a breath that is not there, convinced that something dangerous is about to happen. The need to be on guard all the time has become a second nature, and it exhausts her.

She has stopped walking home alone. She avoids the park near her school. When a police car idles at a stoplight, her stomach drops-not because she has done anything wrong, but because the sight of the uniform pulls her back to that night when the officers told her there was nothing they could do. The feeling of being followed has returned, even when she knows no one is there. She checks her rearview mirror obsessively, circles blocks before parking, and has begun to believe that her life has been destroyed-that the person she was before, the one who laughed easily and trusted strangers, is gone.

The cycle tightens. Every trigger-the heavy breath, the police cruiser, the silence that stretches too long-floods her with fear, and that fear itself brings the memory rushing back in its fragmented, wordless form. Each fragment deepens her conviction that she must stay vigilant, and that vigilance makes her notice more triggers. She is certain that if she lets her guard down, something worse will happen. She has started leaving work early, making excuses to colleagues, and her relationship has grown strained; her boyfriend does not understand why she flinches when he comes up behind her, and she cannot find the words to explain. What finally brought Maya to seek help was the morning she could not bring herself to unlock her classroom door. She stood in the hallway, listening to the silence, and was certain that on the other side of that door, someone was waiting. She is most afraid that she will never feel safe again-and she is hoping, barely, that someone can show her how.
